directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Winter Nelis ripens very late and needs a period of cold storage before it develops its best flavor. An old Belgian variety introduced in the early nineteenth century, it bears small, unassuming, dull green-russeted fruit that belies exceptionally rich, sweet, aromatic flesh once properly ripened, and it was among the most widely planted winter dessert pears in nineteenth-century American orchards for its outstanding flavor and long storage life. Unlike fall-ripening pears such as Bartlett, it needs weeks of cool storage after harvest before the flesh softens and the rich flavor fully develops, rewarding patience with one of the best-flavored of all winter pears. Harvest while still hard and green in mid-to-late fall, store cool for several weeks to a few months, then finish ripening at room temperature for a few days before eating.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer such as Bartlett; Clapp's Favorite ripens quickly once picked and bruises easily, so harvest and handle it gently.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer such as Bartlett; Clapp's Favorite ripens quickly once picked and bruises easily, so harvest and handle it gently. Bred in Massachusetts in the 1860s, it bears large, pale yellow-green pears blushed with red, similar in shape and flavor to Bartlett but ripening about two weeks earlier, with sweet, juicy, fine-textured flesh that made it a widely planted early-season dessert pear in American orchards for well over a century. Its early ripening extends the home orchard's fresh pear season ahead of the main Bartlett crop, though the fruit softens and turns mealy very quickly once ripe and bruises easily, so it needs prompt picking and careful handling compared to firmer, better-keeping pear varieties. Harvest while still firm and green in late summer, then ripen indoors at room temperature and eat promptly once the flesh yields to gentle pressure.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Research and Extension Center

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Forelle is a smaller, ornamental-looking pear well suited to a home orchard with limited space. An old German heirloom pear whose name means trout in German, a reference to the distinctive red speckles that cover its bright yellow skin as it ripens, giving the fruit a striking, ornamental appearance quite different from most solid-colored pears, with crisp, sweet, juicy flesh good for fresh eating. Its small, attractive, speckled fruit and moderate tree size have made it a popular choice for a home orchard wanting an ornamentally distinctive dessert pear alongside its good eating quality. Harvest while still firm and green-yellow in early-to-mid fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for a few days until the flesh yields slightly near the stem.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Research and Extension Center

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Passe Crassane ripens very late and needs weeks of cold storage before the gritty flesh softens and sweetens.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Passe Crassane ripens very late and needs weeks of cold storage before the gritty flesh softens and sweetens. A classic French winter pear bred in Normandy in the mid-nineteenth century, it was for generations the standard Christmas and New Year's market pear across France, bearing large, round, russeted fruit with dense flesh that is notably gritty and unpalatable straight off the tree but softens into rich, sweet, fine-textured flesh after a long period of cold storage. Its very late ripening and exceptional keeping ability once properly stored made it historically important for extending the fresh pear season deep into winter, well after other varieties had finished. Harvest quite late in fall while still very hard, store cool for many weeks, then finish ripening at room temperature until the flesh softens fully before eating.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste
